planting.note: Set rooted divisions directly into saturated mud or shallow standing water in full sun to partial shade; creeping rush roots readily from stem fragments and spreads fastest once water levels stabilize for the season.

directions: Plant in saturated mud or shallow standing water up to a few inches deep in full sun to partial shade; creeping rush naturally occupies the fluctuating-water-level margins of Coastal Plain seasonal ponds and interdunal swales, forming low, wiry, floating-to-prostrate mats rather than upright clumps. It tolerates the boom-and-bust hydrology of these basins, surviving both shallow inundation and brief drawdown by rooting opportunistically at stem nodes wherever they touch wet substrate. Use it along pond margins, rain garden low points, and water-garden edges where a fine-textured, low groundcover rush is wanted instead of a tall upright species. It spreads by rooting stems rather than seed in cultivation, so plugs or divisions establish far faster than sown seed.
sources: Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into saturated, acidic, sandy-peaty soil in full sun; awned meadowbeauty needs the seasonal flood-and-drawdown cycle of a depression pond margin and will decline in permanently dry or permanently flooded ground.

directions: Plant in acidic, sandy, low-nutrient soil that floods seasonally and then draws down in full sun; awned meadowbeauty is a specialist of Coastal Plain depression ponds and Delmarva-type seasonal bays, where it occupies the zone that is submerged in winter and spring but exposed and damp-sandy by late summer bloom time. The slender, bristle-tipped sepal lobes that give the species its name distinguish it from the more common Virginia and Maryland meadowbeauties at close range. Like other Rhexia, its rose-pink flowers are buzz-pollinated by bumblebees and last only a single day each, with new flowers opening daily through the summer bloom period. Recreate its native hydrology in a man-made pond-margin or rain garden basin that cycles between shallow flooding and a damp, sandy drawdown rather than staying uniformly wet or dry.

planting.note: Set nursery-propagated plants in spring into dry, deep, infertile white sand in full sun; Florida golden aster is a federally threatened Pinellas County scrub endemic, so only purchase nursery-grown stock and never collect from the wild.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, infertile white sand in full sun; Florida golden aster is restricted to the ancient relict scrub dunes of Pinellas County, one of the narrowest ranges of any Florida scrub endemic, and is federally listed as threatened due to habitat loss from coastal development. It forms a woody-based perennial clump with felted gray-green leaves and clusters of bright yellow daisy-like flowers that open mainly in fall, standing out against the otherwise sparse, open white-sand scrub. Like other scrub specialists it requires sharp drainage and resents any soil enrichment, irrigation, or shading from encroaching vegetation. It is propagated and planted as part of local scrub restoration efforts, and nursery-grown material is occasionally offered through Florida native plant society chapter sales for scrub and xeriscape gardens.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Recovery Plan

planting.note: Set nursery-grown plants in spring into deep, infertile white sand in full sun; scrub mint is a federally endangered Lake Wales Ridge endemic, so obtain plants only from accredited native plant nurseries or botanical garden sales and never collect from the wild.

directions: Plant in deep, sharply drained, infertile white sand in full sun; scrub mint is endemic to the ancient dune ridge of central Florida's Lake Wales Ridge, one of the most imperiled ecosystems in the country, and is federally listed as endangered because of habitat loss to agriculture and development. The narrow, needle-like, highly aromatic leaves release a pungent minty scent when brushed, and small lavender-pink, spotted-throated flowers appear over a long warm-season bloom period. It depends on the periodic fire and open sandy gaps of scrub habitat and will decline if shaded out by taller shrubs or grown in enriched, moisture-retentive soil. Botanical gardens involved in Lake Wales Ridge conservation occasionally offer nursery-propagated plants at native plant sales for scrub-habitat and xeriscape gardens.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Recovery Plan
Bok Tower Gardens Rare Plant Conservation Program
